description: A 2×2 composite of false-colour two-dimensional SAXS detector images labelled (a)–(d), all sharing the same axes: x (pixels) from 0 to about 480 and y (pixels) 0 to 600. Two full-width horizontal black stripes cross every panel at y ≈ 200 and y ≈ 410 pixels, i.e. masked detector gaps/beamstop shadow. Each panel is dominated by a small dark central disc (beamstop) ringed by a compact red–orange high-intensity ring, which lies inside a broad green halo decaying to blue background at large radius; the pattern is isotropic about the centre, and faint dark specks near the lower edge look like noise. No colour bar, intensity scale, composition label or q axis is printed on any panel, so the colour mapping and the panel-to-composition assignment are not quantitatively readable; the bright ring/green halo appear somewhat larger in (d) than in (a). The caption, however, describes Fig. 3 as radially integrated SAXS intensity profiles of Fe–Al low-density steels with 5–9 wt% Al (open symbols, fitted solid curves), a weak nano-sized ordered-phase peak at q = 0.3–3 nm⁻¹ and a q⁻⁴ decay below 0.3 nm⁻¹, reporting Fe₃Al ordered-phase diameters of 2.5 ± 0.15 to 3.75 ± 0.2 nm; those curves, symbols and numbers are not present in the supplied pixels.
measured_quantities: 2D SAXS scattering intensity (arbitrary units, colour-coded; no colour bar shown)
scattering vector q (nm⁻¹) — stated in caption, not plotted in the supplied pixels
ordered-phase volume fraction — stated in caption

observations.observation: The image group consists of four false-colour 2D SAXS detector patterns labelled (a)–(d), each plotted with axes x (pixels) 0–~480 and y (pixels) 0–600.
Two full-width horizontal black stripes cross every panel at y ≈ 200 and y ≈ 410 pixels, consistent with masked detector gaps or beamstop shadows.

Each panel shows a small dark central disc surrounded by a compact red–orange high-intensity ring embedded in a broad green halo that decays to blue background at large radius, i.e. an isotropic scattering ring about the beam centre.
The bright ring and green halo appear progressively larger from (a) through (d), with (d) showing the most extended halo and (a) the most compact.
No colour bar, intensity scale, q axis, composition label or scale bar is printed on any panel, so the colour-to-intensity mapping and the Al content of each panel cannot be read from the pixels.
Faint dark specks are visible near the lower edge of the panels (e.g. around x ≈ 350, y ≈ 30 pixels in (a)) and are not labelled; they appear to be detector noise or artefacts.
The caption states the panels refer to Fe–Al low-density steels with increasing Al content from 5 to 9 wt%.
The caption states that a weak peak from the nano-sized ordered phase is observed between q = 0.3–3 nm⁻¹.

The caption states that scattering intensity increases with Al content, implying an increase of the nano-sized ordered phase, and that the Guinier regions shift towards low q, confirming an increase in ordered-phase size.

The caption states that below q = 0.3 nm⁻¹ the intensity decays as q⁻⁴, attributed to larger heterogeneities such as grains and/or grain boundaries, and that above q = 3 nm⁻¹ the intensity is an incoherent flat background.
The caption states the Fe₃Al ordered-phase diameter increased from 2.5 ± 0.15 nm to 3.75 ± 0.2 nm with increasing Al content.

The caption states the ordered-phase volume fractions measured by SAXS are lower than the DO₃ fraction from Mössbauer spectroscopy because SAXS senses ordered phase with sharper boundaries while Mössbauer traces all local environments including diffuse boundaries.

Caption–image disagreement: the caption describes Fig. 3 as radially integrated SAXS intensity (open symbols) with fitted solid curves versus q, but the supplied pixels show false-colour 2D SAXS detector images containing no data symbols, no fitted curves and no q axis.
